newsitem.title: ITALY: Gucci loosens up, widens cut in menswear.
newsitem.headline: Gucci loosens up, widens cut in menswear.

text.p: Italian fashion house Gucci broadened shoulders and elongated jacket lengths in its 1997/98 autumn/winter menswear show on Tuesday, imbuing the ready-to-wear collection with a loose and casual air.
Gucci designer Tom Ford presented a smoothly coordinated line-up, keeping suit and shirt colours to the same hue and concealing jacket and coat buttons on the inside of the garment.

Trousers were slack at the hip, belted and wide from the top of the thigh almost to the floor while suit jackets were generous at the shoulder but not heavily structured, loosely tailored at the waist and in some cases extending to the knee.
Midnight blue, slate grey or chocolate dominated in suede, silk and velvet, where the Gucci GG symbol formed the pattern, and in fine round-collared knits and wider meshed turtle necks.
Vibrant splashes of colour came in red or brown silk shirts with a silver paisley print or monotone red, green or blue shot silk paired with green-blue paintbrush marked pants.
Italian Gianfranco Ferre displayed an upbeat second line for the young and sporty under his Gieffeffe label, with jackets and pants aimed at versatility and practicality.
Ice white or lava black stirrup pants and same colour boxy, short cropped jackets trimmed with fur collars and cuffs were worn with thick soled boots.
Ribbed knits in black and white check reinforced the image of winter warmth while Ferre ensured a variety of duster coats, windbreakers, bomber jackets and parkas to suit all needs.
A thick cream scarf slung from the neck with two edges stitched together behind became a halterneck waistcoat buttoned at the front and tasselled at the hem like a real scarf.

Ferre also showed warm orange corduroy jackets and wide-legged trousers hemmed above the ankle and more subtle-hued olive or khaki pants and jackets, some lightly elasticated at the waist and others buttoned high in the style of a shirt.

Briton Vivienne Westwood reverted to the 16th century codpiece and hose in her line-up late on Monday night, recreating the Tudor dress of English King Henry VIII with puff sleeves on doublet-style jackets and men in tights.
Puffball breeches in slashed red satin stopped at the thigh, a red and grey sectioned skintight jumpsuit tied across the hip and trousers came with unstructured codpiece-style front panels.

Italian design house Fendi stuck to the 20th century with sophisticated designs in browns and greys. The overall silhouette was slender, with trousers straight and narrow or slightly bagged and gathered at the ankle like golfing pants.
For men wanting ties there were monochrome and floral prints but for those joining a growing trend towards suits without ties came fine-knit jersey shirts with collars in chocolate or grey.
Suits came in two and three pieces while evening dress included burgundy velvet waistcoats, black velvet jackets and close-fitting trousers with a double stripe down the side.
The shows, which run until Thursday, have drawn few famous names but actor Larry Hagman, "J.R." in the 1980s U.S. television series Dallas, attended a presentation by Gianni Campagna.
